name: Enterprise Design Patterns

beginner.content:
What is the MVC Pattern?

MVC (Model-View-Controller) splits an application into three interconnected parts so that each concern - data, presentation, and control flow - can change independently without breaking the others.

• Model - holds the application's data and business logic (e.g. a User or Order class).
• View - renders the data to the user (an HTML page, JSON response, or console output).
• Controller - receives input, talks to the Model, and picks which View to render.

Why Split Things Up?

Without MVC, a single class ends up doing data access, business rules, and rendering all at once - a change to the UI risks breaking business logic, and vice versa. MVC isolates each responsibility so multiple people can work on the same app without stepping on each other.

expert.content:
MVC in Real Frameworks - Spring MVC

Spring MVC is a concrete, industry-standard implementation of this pattern:

• A @Controller/@RestController class receives the HTTP request.
• It calls a Service layer, which operates on Model objects (entities/DTOs).
• It returns a logical view name (for server-rendered pages) or the Model data directly as JSON (for REST APIs), and Spring's DispatcherServlet (a Front Controller) resolves and renders the actual View.

So "MVC" in a Spring app isn't just a naming convention - it's this exact separation, enforced by the framework's own request-handling pipeline.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does MVC solve?It separates data, presentation, and control flow so each can change independently, improving maintainability and enabling parallel development
What is the Controller's job?Receiving input/requests, coordinating with the Model, and selecting which View renders the response - it should not contain business logic itself
How does Spring MVC implement this pattern?DispatcherServlet acts as the entry point (Front Controller), delegates to @Controller classes, which use Service/Model layers and return a View name or data
Can the View talk directly to the Model?In classic Smalltalk-80 MVC the View holds a reference to the Model, observes it directly and is notified of changes. It is WEB (Model-2) MVC where the Controller assembles model data and hands it to the View. Either way the View shouldn't mutate the Model or contain business logic

beginner.content:
What is the Front Controller Pattern?

A Front Controller is a single, centralized entry point that handles every incoming request for an application, before dispatching it to the right handler. Instead of every page/servlet independently doing authentication, logging, and routing, one component does it once, consistently, for all requests.

Without a Front Controller

Each servlet/page repeats the same boilerplate: check login, log the request, pick a view, handle errors - duplicated everywhere, easy to get inconsistent.

With a Front Controller

One controller intercepts every request, performs the shared logic once, then delegates to a specific handler for that request's actual business work.

expert.content:
Real-World Front Controllers

• Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet is a textbook Front Controller - every HTTP request for the app passes through it first, and it delegates to the matching @Controller method.
• Servlet Filter chains can also implement cross-cutting Front-Controller-style behavior (auth, logging, CORS) applied uniformly before requests reach any servlet.

The benefit compounds as an application grows: adding a new cross-cutting concern (e.g. rate limiting) means changing ONE place instead of every page/handler.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a Front Controller?A single centralized entry point for all requests, which performs shared logic (auth, logging) once and then delegates to specific handlers
Name a real Front Controller in Java web frameworksSpring MVC's DispatcherServlet
What's the main benefit over per-page handling?Shared/cross-cutting logic lives in one place instead of being duplicated (and potentially inconsistent) across every page/servlet

beginner.content:
What is the Page Controller Pattern?

A Page Controller assigns one controller class (or method) per page or request type - each controller handles exactly one kind of request end-to-end, from input to choosing the response. This is the direct opposite structural choice from Front Controller's single shared entry point.

When It Fits

• Simple sites/apps with a small, fixed set of distinct pages, where each page's logic is genuinely independent.
• Easier to understand for a single page in isolation - there's no shared dispatch machinery to trace through.

When It Doesn't Scale Well

Cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging) must be repeated in every Page Controller, unless you also introduce a Front Controller or Filter layer on top - which is exactly why real frameworks combine both (Front Controller for shared concerns, Page-Controller-like @Controller methods for specific request handling).

expert.content:
Page Controller vs Front Controller

AspectPage ControllerFront Controller
Entry pointsOne controller per page/request typeA single shared entry point for all requests
Cross-cutting logicRepeated per controller unless factored out separatelyCentralized once
Best fitSmall apps, few distinct simple pagesLarger apps needing consistent shared behavior

In practice, Spring MVC's individual @Controller methods act like Page Controllers for their specific routes, while DispatcherServlet still serves as the overarching Front Controller - the two patterns are commonly combined, not mutually exclusive.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does Page Controller differ from Front Controller?Page Controller assigns one handler per page/request type; Front Controller routes all requests through one shared entry point
Are the two patterns mutually exclusive?No - Spring MVC combines both: DispatcherServlet is the Front Controller, and individual @Controller methods act like Page Controllers per route

beginner.content:
What is the Application Controller Pattern?

An Application Controller centralizes screen/view navigation and command-selection logic in one place, separate from the Front Controller. The Front Controller handles "which request came in", while the Application Controller handles "given this action, which view/command comes next" - useful when navigation flow is complex (e.g. multi-step wizards, workflow-driven UIs).

expert.content:
Application Controller vs Front Controller

These are complementary, not competing: the Front Controller is the single request entry point (handles EVERY incoming request); the Application Controller is invoked BY specific handlers to decide navigation/command flow when that flow is non-trivial (e.g. depends on prior steps, user role, or business state). Simple apps skip a dedicated Application Controller entirely and let each handler pick its own next view directly.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does an Application Controller centralize?Navigation/command-selection logic - deciding which view or command comes next given the current action/state
How is it different from a Front Controller?Front Controller handles every incoming request as the entry point; Application Controller is about deciding navigation flow once inside request handling
When is a dedicated Application Controller worth it?When navigation logic is complex (multi-step wizards, workflow/state-dependent screens) - simple apps can let each handler pick its own next view

beginner.content:
What is the Service Layer Pattern?

A Service Layer is a dedicated layer that defines an application's business-logic boundary/API. Controllers call into Service classes; Service classes coordinate domain objects, repositories, and (often) transactions - keeping business rules out of the Controller and out of raw data-access code.

Why It Matters

• Controllers stay thin - just translating HTTP requests into service calls.
• Business logic lives in ONE testable, reusable place instead of being scattered across controllers or duplicated per entry point (web, batch job, CLI all reuse the same Service).
• Transaction boundaries (commit/rollback) typically wrap a Service method, not individual repository calls.

expert.content:
Service Layer in Spring

Spring's @Service annotation marks a class as this exact layer. Combined with @Transactional on a Service method, Spring wraps that entire method - including all its repository calls - in a single database transaction, so a failure partway through rolls back everything cleanly. This is precisely why business logic and transaction boundaries belong at the Service layer, not scattered in Controllers or Repositories.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What belongs in a Service Layer?Business logic and orchestration between domain objects/repositories - not raw data access, not HTTP/request handling
Why keep Controllers thin?So business logic is reusable across multiple entry points (web, batch, CLI) and is easier to unit test in isolation from HTTP concerns
Where do transaction boundaries typically live?Around Service methods (e.g. @Transactional), so a whole business operation commits or rolls back as one unit

beginner.content:
What is the Domain Model Pattern?

A Domain Model is an object model of the business domain that combines BOTH data AND behavior in the same objects - a BankAccount class doesn't just hold a balance field, it also has a withdraw() method that enforces the business rule (can't go below zero) directly on itself.

Domain Model vs Anemic Domain Model

An anemic domain model (an anti-pattern, not this pattern) has classes that are just data bags (getters/setters only), with ALL logic living in separate Service classes. A true Domain Model pushes behavior that belongs to the data onto the data's own class.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What defines a (rich) Domain Model?Objects that combine data AND behavior - business rules live as methods on the objects they protect, not in a separate service only
What is an anemic domain model?An anti-pattern where domain classes are pure getter/setter data bags, with all logic pushed into external Service classes - loses encapsulation of business rules
What's the risk of an anemic model?Business rules can be bypassed by any code that calls the setters directly, since the object itself doesn't enforce its own invariants

beginner.content:
What is the Transaction Script Pattern?

Transaction Script organizes business logic as a set of procedural methods/scripts - one script per business transaction/use-case (e.g. placeOrder(), cancelOrder()), each running top-to-bottom: validate input, do the work, save results. There's no rich object model - just straightforward procedures operating on simple data.

When It Fits

Great for simple applications with straightforward, mostly-independent business rules - it's easy to read top-to-bottom and quick to write. It intentionally trades object-oriented elegance for procedural simplicity.

When It Breaks Down

As business rules grow more complex and start overlapping between transactions, logic gets duplicated across scripts (since there's no shared object to hold it) - that's exactly the point where a Domain Model pays off instead.

expert.content:
Transaction Script vs Domain Model

AspectTransaction ScriptDomain Model
StructureProcedural methods, one per use-caseRich objects with behavior + data
Best forSimple, largely-independent business rulesComplex, interrelated business rules
Code reuse across use-casesHard - logic duplicates across scriptsNatural - shared logic lives on shared objects
Learning curveLow - reads top-to-bottomHigher - requires understanding object collaboration

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is Transaction Script?Organizing business logic as procedural methods, one per business transaction, executed top-to-bottom
When does it break down?When business rules overlap across transactions - logic ends up duplicated since there's no shared domain object to hold it
What's the natural next step when complexity grows?Migrating shared logic into a Domain Model, where behavior lives on the objects it operates on instead of in disconnected scripts

beginner.content:
What is the Repository Pattern?

A Repository mediates between the domain/business layer and the data-mapping layer, exposing a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects - callers work with methods like findById(), save(), findAll() as if they were querying an in-memory collection, without knowing or caring whether the data actually comes from a database, a file, or an in-memory cache.

Why It's Useful

• The rest of the application depends only on the Repository's interface, not on SQL/JDBC/JPA details.
• Swapping the underlying storage (e.g. moving from an in-memory list to a real database) means changing ONE implementation, not every caller.
• Makes unit testing easy - swap in a fake/in-memory Repository implementation instead of hitting a real database.

expert.content:
Repository vs DAO

The two are closely related and often conflated, but conceptually differ in intent:

• DAO (Data Access Object) is typically table/entity-centric - it directly wraps CRUD operations against one specific data source (SQL statements, JDBC calls).
• Repository is domain-centric - it presents a collection-like abstraction over the domain model, and may internally delegate to one or more DAOs. Repository sits one level of abstraction higher, closer to the business/domain language.

In modern Spring applications, Spring Data JPA repositories (interfaces extending JpaRepository<Entity, ID>) blur this line further - you get a full Repository-style API auto-implemented for you, backed by JPA/Hibernate underneath. A dedicated "DAO" topic elsewhere covers the lower-level data-access details in depth.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does a Repository abstract away?The underlying data source/storage mechanism - callers use a collection-like API without knowing if data comes from SQL, a file, or memory
How is Repository different from DAO?DAO is typically table/entity-centric CRUD wrapping one data source directly; Repository is domain-centric and may compose multiple DAOs behind a collection-like abstraction
Why does this pattern make testing easier?Since code depends on the Repository interface, tests can substitute an in-memory fake implementation instead of needing a real database
How does Spring Data JPA relate to this pattern?It auto-generates Repository implementations from interfaces (e.g. extending JpaRepository), backed by JPA/Hibernate, so you get the pattern's benefits with minimal boilerplate

beginner.content:
What is the DAO Pattern?

A Data Access Object (DAO) abstracts and encapsulates all access to a data source (a database, a file, a web service) behind a well-defined interface. The rest of the application talks to the DAO's interface only - it never writes SQL or touches a Connection object directly.

• Keeps persistence-specific code (JDBC, SQL) isolated in one layer.
• If the storage technology changes (JDBC -> JPA, MySQL -> PostgreSQL), only the DAO implementation changes - callers are untouched.
• Makes unit testing easier - a service can be tested against a fake/mock DAO without hitting a real database.

expert.content:
DAO vs Repository

These two patterns are frequently confused because both hide persistence details behind an interface, but they solve slightly different problems:

AspectDAORepository
FocusTable/entity-centric CRUD operationsCollection-like abstraction over the domain model
Typical shapesave(), findById(), delete(), update()add(), remove(), findByX() - reads like an in-memory collection
OriginJ2EE Core Patterns (data-access layer concern)Domain-Driven Design (a domain-layer concept)
Java exampleA plain DAO interface + JDBC implementationSpring Data JPA's JpaRepository<T, ID>

In practice, Spring Data repositories are often DAOs wearing a Repository-shaped interface - the distinction matters more in strict DDD architectures than in typical Spring Boot CRUD apps.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does DAO solve?It isolates all data-access/persistence code behind one interface, so the rest of the app doesn't depend on a specific storage technology
How does DAO help testing?Services can depend on the DAO interface and be tested with a fake/in-memory/mock implementation instead of a real database
DAO vs Repository - what's the core difference?DAO is table/entity-centric CRUD; Repository is a collection-like abstraction over the domain, a Domain-Driven Design concept
Is Spring Data JPA's JpaRepository a DAO?Functionally yes - it implements CRUD/data-access behind an interface, just using Repository-style naming/semantics

beginner.content:
What is the Data Mapper Pattern?

A Data Mapper is a separate layer of objects that moves data between plain domain objects and a database, while keeping the domain objects, the database schema, and the mapper itself completely independent of each other.

• The domain object (e.g. Employee) has NO idea a database exists - no save()/find() methods on it, no SQL, no JDBC imports.
• The Mapper is the only thing that knows how to translate between the object's fields and the database columns.
• This separation is exactly what Hibernate/JPA implement internally: your @Entity classes stay plain Java objects, and Hibernate's session/EntityManager acts as the Data Mapper.

expert.content:
Data Mapper in Hibernate/JPA

When you annotate a class with @Entity and call entityManager.persist(employee), Hibernate's persistence context is playing the role of the Data Mapper: it reads your entity's fields via reflection, generates the SQL, and writes it to the database - your Employee class itself stays a Plain Old Java Object with zero SQL inside it. This is why JPA entities can be unit-tested with plain new Employee(...) calls, no database required.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the core idea of Data Mapper?Move data between objects and the database through a separate mapper layer, keeping domain objects, schema, and mapper all independent of each other
Does the domain object know about the database in Data Mapper?No - that's the whole point; the domain object stays a plain object with no persistence logic inside it
Which real Java technology implements Data Mapper?Hibernate/JPA - the EntityManager/Session acts as the mapper, while @Entity classes remain plain objects

beginner.content:
What is the Active Record Pattern?

An Active Record object wraps a single row of a database table AND encapsulates the database-access logic (save, delete, find) inside that SAME class. Unlike Data Mapper, the domain object here is fully aware it's persisted - it knows how to save/load/delete itself.

expert.content:
Active Record vs Data Mapper

AspectActive RecordData Mapper
Persistence logic lives inThe domain object itself (save()/delete())A separate Mapper class
Domain object aware of DB?Yes - tightly coupled to persistenceNo - stays a plain object
SimplicitySimpler for small/CRUD-heavy appsMore boilerplate, but cleaner separation
TestabilityHarder - object drags in persistence behaviorEasier - pure domain object, no persistence dependency
Java examplesSome lightweight ORMs / ActiveJDBC-style librariesHibernate/JPA

Active Record trades architectural purity for simplicity - a reasonable choice for small apps with simple, mostly-CRUD domain logic; it becomes a liability as business logic complexity grows.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What defines Active Record?A single class holds both the row's data AND the logic to save/load/delete that row itself
Why is Active Record harder to unit test than Data Mapper?Because the domain object is coupled to persistence logic, so testing pure business rules also drags in database behavior
When is Active Record a reasonable choice?Small applications with simple, mostly-CRUD domain logic where the extra separation of Data Mapper isn't worth the boilerplate

beginner.content:
What is the Unit of Work Pattern?

A Unit of Work keeps track of everything you do during a business transaction - every object created, updated, or deleted - and then coordinates writing all of it out as one atomic operation at the end, instead of firing off a database call for every single change immediately.

• Batches changes together for one commit, instead of many small round-trips.
• Lets you roll back the entire set of changes together if anything fails.

expert.content:
Unit of Work in Hibernate

Hibernate's Session (or JPA's EntityManager within a persistence context) is a real Unit of Work: entities you load, modify, or persist are tracked in the session's internal state, and nothing actually hits the database until flush()/commit() - at which point Hibernate computes the minimal set of INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements needed and executes them together. This is also what enables Hibernate's automatic "dirty checking" - it compares an entity's current state to its loaded snapshot to know what changed, without you calling any explicit registerDirty()-style method.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Unit of Work solve?Coordinating many pending changes as one atomic commit instead of many separate database round-trips
What plays the role of Unit of Work in Hibernate?The Session/EntityManager - it tracks changes and flushes them together at commit time
How does Hibernate know what changed without explicit registerDirty() calls?Automatic dirty checking - it compares the entity's current field values against the snapshot taken when it was loaded

beginner.content:
What is the Identity Map Pattern?

An Identity Map ensures each object is loaded only once per session, by keeping a map of already-loaded objects keyed by their identity (usually the primary key). If the same row is requested again within the same session, the cached in-memory object is returned instead of hitting the database and creating a second, separate copy.

• Prevents having two different in-memory objects representing the same database row (which could drift out of sync).
• Improves performance by avoiding redundant database reads within one session.

expert.content:
Identity Map in Hibernate

Hibernate's first-level cache (scoped to a single Session) IS an Identity Map: loading the same entity by id twice within one session returns the exact same Java object reference the second time, without a second SQL query. This is also why comparing two entities loaded in the same session with == works correctly for identity, in addition to equals().

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What does an Identity Map guarantee?Only one in-memory object exists per unique database row identity within a session, avoiding duplicate/inconsistent copies
What plays this role in Hibernate?The first-level cache (Session-scoped) - repeated find-by-id calls return the same object reference without hitting the DB again

beginner.content:
What is the Business Delegate Pattern?

A Business Delegate is an object that hides the complexity of looking up and invoking a remote/complex business service (classically, an EJB lookup via JNDI) from the presentation-tier client. The client talks to a simple delegate; the delegate handles lookup, invocation, and even basic error/retry handling.

• Decouples the presentation layer from the business-service layer's implementation details.
• Centralizes lookup/connection logic in one place instead of scattering it across every UI action.

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does Business Delegate solve?It hides remote/complex business-service lookup and invocation details from the presentation-tier client, reducing coupling
Where did this pattern originate?Classic J2EE, originally to hide EJB (JNDI) lookup complexity from UI/servlet code
Is Business Delegate still relevant in modern Spring apps?Less commonly needed by that name since Spring's dependency injection already hides lookup complexity, but the underlying idea (decoupling presentation from service lookup) still applies

beginner.content:
What is the Session Facade Pattern?

A Session Facade is a coarse-grained facade that exposes a simplified, unified interface to a set of fine-grained business objects, specifically for remote/presentation-tier clients. It's essentially the classic GoF Facade pattern, specialized for J2EE's remote-service-access context.

• Reduces the number of remote calls a client needs to make (one call to the facade instead of many calls to fine-grained objects).
• Hides the internal complexity/structure of the business-object model from remote clients.

expert.content:
Session Facade vs Plain Facade (GoF)

Session Facade IS the GoF Facade pattern - the distinction is purely about context, not mechanics: the classic Facade pattern simplifies a subsystem for ANY client, while Session Facade specifically addresses reducing remote call overhead for presentation-tier clients talking to distributed/remote business objects (historically EJBs). In a modern non-distributed Spring app, a @Service class that coordinates several other services already plays this role without needing the "Session" qualifier.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How is Session Facade different from the GoF Facade pattern?It isn't structurally different - it's the same idea specialized for reducing remote-call overhead to distributed business objects (classically EJBs) for presentation-tier clients
What's the main benefit for a remote client?Fewer remote round-trips - one call to the facade instead of many calls to fine-grained remote objects

cheatNotes: MVC - separates Model (data), View (presentation), Controller (control flow)
Front Controller - single entry point for all requests (e.g. Spring DispatcherServlet)
Page Controller - one controller per page/request type
Service Layer - defines the business-logic boundary; keeps Controllers thin
Domain Model - rich objects with data + behavior together; opposite of anemic model
Transaction Script - procedural, one method per business transaction; simple but doesn't scale to complex rules
Repository - collection-like abstraction over data access; Repository is domain-centric, DAO is data-source-centric
